sets.title: A choice for our town
sets.summary: Students listen to two classmates argue for different town projects and answer questions about claims, evidence and how a community makes a decision, focusing on argument language such as I think, however and but.

script.title: Crosswalk or Bike Path?
script.setting: A teacher leads a class discussion about a decision the town council must make.

lines.speaker: Ms. Haddad
lines.text: Today we are studying how a community makes decisions. Our town council has money for 1 new project near our school. They asked students for ideas.

lines.speaker: Ms. Haddad
lines.text: Look at the map. Option 1 is a new crosswalk on Maple Street. Option 2 is a bike path along the river. Listen to both sides.

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.text: I think the town should build the crosswalk. Maple Street is very busy in the morning. Last month, our class counted 85 cars in 10 minutes. Many students walk across that street.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: I agree that safety matters. However, I think the bike path is a better choice. Right now, only 12 students ride bikes to school because there is no safe path. A path would help more people get exercise.

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.text: But a bike path only helps students who ride bikes. A crosswalk helps almost everyone who walks, and 140 students walk to school.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: That is true. Still, a bike path could also be used by families on weekends.

lines.speaker: Ms. Haddad
lines.text: You both gave reasons and evidence. Next, the council will hold a public meeting. People will share their opinions, and then the council will vote.

items.stem: What does Kenji want the town to build?

choices.text: A bike path
choices.why: A bike path is the other student's choice.
choices.misconception: Mixes up the two speakers

choices.text: A crosswalk
choices.why: Kenji says, I think the town should build the crosswalk.

choices.text: A new school
choices.why: No one asks for a new school in the discussion.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

items.stem: Where would the bike path go?

choices.text: Along the river
choices.why: The teacher says option 2 is a bike path along the river.

choices.text: On Maple Street
choices.why: Maple Street is the place for the other option.
choices.misconception: Matches a place to the wrong option

choices.text: Behind the school
choices.why: The talk does not say anything about behind the school.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

items.stem: What evidence does Kenji give that Maple Street is busy?

choices.text: His class counted 12 bikes in 10 minutes.
choices.why: The number 12 is about something else, and Kenji did not count bikes.
choices.misconception: Mixes up numbers from different parts of the talk

choices.text: Families use the street on weekends.
choices.why: Weekends come up in the other student's argument, not as evidence about traffic.
choices.misconception: Gives one speaker's point to the other speaker

choices.text: His class counted 85 cars in 10 minutes.
choices.why: Kenji uses the car count from his class as his evidence.

choices.text: The council said the street is busy.
choices.why: Kenji does not say the council told them this.
choices.misconception: Adds a source that was not said

items.stem: According to Priya, why do only 12 students ride bikes to school now?

choices.text: Most students live too far away.
choices.why: Priya does not talk about how far students live.
choices.misconception: Adds a reason that was not said

choices.text: Maple Street has too many cars.
choices.why: The cars are part of Kenji's argument, not Priya's reason about bikes.
choices.misconception: Connects two ideas the speakers did not connect

choices.text: Students do not like exercise.
choices.why: Priya actually says a path would help people get exercise.
choices.misconception: Reverses what the speaker said

choices.text: There is no safe path for bikes.
choices.why: Priya says only 12 students ride because there is no safe path.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why Kenji thinks the crosswalk would help more people?

choices.text: Many more students walk to school than ride bikes.
choices.why: Kenji compares the number of walkers with the number of bike riders to show more people would use the crosswalk.

choices.text: A crosswalk costs less money than a bike path.
choices.why: Cost is never compared in the discussion.
choices.misconception: Adds a reason that sounds logical but was not said

choices.text: Families would use the crosswalk on weekends.
choices.why: The weekend idea was said about the bike path, not the crosswalk.
choices.misconception: Attaches a detail to the wrong option

choices.text: Bikes are not safe on any street in town.
choices.why: No one says bikes are unsafe on every street.
choices.misconception: Over-generalizes from one detail

items.stem: Why will the council hold a public meeting before it votes?

choices.text: So the students can vote on the project
choices.why: The teacher says the council will vote, not the students.
choices.misconception: Confuses who makes the final decision

choices.text: So people in the community can share their opinions first
choices.why: The teacher says people will share their opinions, and then the council will vote.

choices.text: Because the council already chose the crosswalk
choices.why: The talk does not say the council has chosen yet.
choices.misconception: Jumps to a conclusion that was not said

choices.text: To count the cars on Maple Street again
choices.why: Counting cars was a class activity, not the reason for the meeting.
choices.misconception: Connects unrelated details

sets.title: What sticks to a magnet?
sets.summary: Students listen to a group report on a magnet investigation and answer questions about results, predictions and evidence, focusing on sequence words and the language of science reports.

script.title: Testing Objects with a Magnet
script.setting: Two students share the results of a magnet investigation with their teacher and class.

lines.speaker: Mr. Novak
lines.text: Today we tested 6 objects with a bar magnet. We used the same magnet for every object to keep the test fair. Before we started, each group made a prediction. Lucia, please share your group's results.

lines.speaker: Lucia
lines.text: Sure. First, we tested a paper clip. The magnet pulled it right away. Next, we tried a steel spoon. It stuck to the magnet too.

lines.speaker: Lucia
lines.text: Then we tested a coin, a plastic button, a wood block, and an aluminum can. None of those 4 objects stuck.

lines.speaker: Dev
lines.text: We were surprised by the can. We predicted that all metal objects would stick. However, the aluminum can did not move at all.

lines.speaker: Mr. Novak
lines.text: That is an important observation. Magnets attract some metals, like iron and steel. They do not attract every metal. Aluminum and copper are metals, but magnets do not pull them.

lines.speaker: Dev
lines.text: So our prediction was wrong. We should change it to say that only some metals stick to magnets.

lines.speaker: Mr. Novak
lines.text: Exactly. Scientists change their ideas when the evidence shows something new. Tomorrow, you will test 6 new objects and record the results in a table.

items.stem: Which object did the group test first?

choices.text: A paper clip
choices.why: Lucia says, first, we tested a paper clip.

choices.text: A steel spoon
choices.why: The group tested the spoon next, not first.
choices.misconception: Confuses the order of events

choices.text: A wood block
choices.why: The wood block was tested later in the investigation.
choices.misconception: Picks a detail that was said but does not answer

items.stem: What tool did the class use to test the objects?

choices.text: A scale
choices.why: A scale measures weight, and the class did not weigh anything.
choices.misconception: Confuses testing with measuring weight

choices.text: A ruler
choices.why: The talk does not mention a ruler.
choices.misconception: Adds a common science tool that was not named

choices.text: A magnet
choices.why: The teacher says they tested the objects with a bar magnet.

items.stem: How many of the 6 objects did NOT stick to the magnet?

choices.text: 2 objects
choices.why: 2 is the number of objects that did stick.
choices.misconception: Counts the opposite group

choices.text: 4 objects
choices.why: Lucia names 4 objects that did not stick, and 6 take away the 2 that stuck is 4.

choices.text: 6 objects
choices.why: 6 is the total number of objects tested.
choices.misconception: Gives the total instead of a part

choices.text: 1 object
choices.why: The can was surprising, but it was not the only object that did not stick.
choices.misconception: Focuses only on the most surprising detail

items.stem: Why was Dev's group surprised by the aluminum can?

choices.text: The can stuck to the magnet very fast.
choices.why: Dev says the can did not move at all.
choices.misconception: Reverses the result that was said

choices.text: The can was the heaviest object.
choices.why: No one talks about how heavy the objects were.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

choices.text: The magnet broke when it touched the can.
choices.why: Nothing in the talk says the magnet broke.
choices.misconception: Invents an event that was not said

choices.text: They thought all metal would stick, but the can did not.
choices.why: Dev says they predicted all metal objects would stick, but the can did not move.

items.stem: What is the main science idea Mr. Novak wants students to learn?

choices.text: Magnets attract all metal objects.
choices.why: This was the group's first prediction, and the evidence showed it was not true.
choices.misconception: Keeps the original prediction instead of the conclusion

choices.text: Magnets attract plastic and wood.
choices.why: The plastic button and wood block did not stick.
choices.misconception: Reverses the results

choices.text: Magnets attract some metals, but not all metals.
choices.why: The teacher explains that magnets pull iron and steel but not every metal.

choices.text: Steel is stronger than aluminum.
choices.why: The talk is about which objects a magnet pulls, not which metal is stronger.
choices.misconception: Draws a conclusion about a different idea

items.stem: Why does Mr. Novak say it is good that Dev's group changed its prediction?

choices.text: Good scientists update their ideas to match the evidence.
choices.why: The teacher says scientists change their ideas when the evidence shows something new.

choices.text: A prediction is only good if it is right the first time.
choices.why: The teacher praises the group for changing a prediction that was wrong.
choices.misconception: Reverses the speaker's point

choices.text: The group needed a new magnet for the next test.
choices.why: The class used the same magnet, and no one says they need a new one.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

choices.text: Changing a prediction makes the results come out the same.
choices.why: Changing a prediction does not change what the magnet does.
choices.misconception: Confuses a prediction with a result

sets.title: Directions for the recycling team
sets.summary: Students listen to multi-step classroom directions for setting up a recycling station and answer questions about order, location and purpose, focusing on sequence words and reasons with because and so.

script.title: Setting Up the Recycling Station
script.setting: A teacher gives directions to a student team before they start a school job.

lines.speaker: Ms. Mensah
lines.text: Good morning, recycling team. This week, you will set up a new recycling station in the cafeteria. Please listen carefully, because the steps go in order.

lines.speaker: Ms. Mensah
lines.text: First, pick up 3 bins from the supply room. The blue bin is for paper. The green bin is for plastic bottles. The gray bin is for food scraps that go to the school garden.

lines.speaker: Ms. Mensah
lines.text: Next, place the bins next to the cafeteria door, not by the windows. Students pass the door on their way out, so they will see the bins.

lines.speaker: Ms. Mensah
lines.text: After that, tape a sign with a picture above each bin. Pictures help younger students and new students who are still learning English.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Ms. Mensah, what should we do if someone puts trash in the wrong bin?

lines.speaker: Ms. Mensah
lines.text: Good question, Omar. Do not take things out with your hands. Instead, tell the lunch helper, and she will fix it with gloves.

lines.speaker: Ms. Mensah
lines.text: Finally, on Friday, count how many bottles are in the green bin. Write the number on our class chart. We want to see if the station makes a difference.

items.stem: Where will the team set up the recycling station?

visual.alt: A recycling sign and a trash can

choices.text: In the cafeteria
choices.why: The teacher says the station will be in the cafeteria.

choices.text: In the supply room
choices.why: The supply room is where the team picks up the bins.
choices.misconception: Picks a place that was said but does not answer

choices.text: In the school garden
choices.why: The garden is where the food scraps go later.
choices.misconception: Picks a place that was said but does not answer

items.stem: Which bin is for plastic bottles?

visual.alt: A recycling sign and a water drop

choices.text: The blue bin
choices.why: The blue bin is for paper.
choices.misconception: Matches a color to the wrong item

choices.text: The gray bin
choices.why: The gray bin is for food scraps.
choices.misconception: Matches a color to the wrong item

choices.text: The green bin
choices.why: The teacher says the green bin is for plastic bottles.

items.stem: What should the team do right after they place the bins by the door?

choices.text: Pick up 3 bins from the supply room.
choices.why: This is the first step, so it happens before placing the bins.
choices.misconception: Confuses the order of steps

choices.text: Tape a sign with a picture above each bin.
choices.why: The teacher says, after that, tape a sign with a picture above each bin.

choices.text: Count the bottles in the green bin.
choices.why: Counting is the last step, on Friday.
choices.misconception: Confuses the order of steps

choices.text: Move the bins next to the windows.
choices.why: The teacher says not to put the bins by the windows.
choices.misconception: Reverses a direction that was given

items.stem: Why should the bins go next to the cafeteria door?

choices.text: Students pass the door when they leave, so they will see the bins.
choices.why: The teacher says students pass the door on their way out, so they will see the bins.

choices.text: The door is close to the supply room.
choices.why: The teacher does not say where the supply room is.
choices.misconception: Adds a reason that was not said

choices.text: The windows are too sunny for the bins.
choices.why: The talk says not to use the windows but does not say they are sunny.
choices.misconception: Invents a reason for a detail that was said

choices.text: The lunch helper stands by the door.
choices.why: The lunch helper is part of a different direction.
choices.misconception: Connects unrelated details

items.stem: What can you infer about why Ms. Mensah tells the team not to take things out of the bins with their hands?

choices.text: She wants the team to finish the job faster.
choices.why: Speed is not part of this direction.
choices.misconception: Adds a purpose that was not suggested

choices.text: The lunch helper does not want any help.
choices.why: The teacher tells the team to ask the helper, so the helper does want to know.
choices.misconception: Over-interprets one detail

choices.text: Things in the wrong bin should stay there.
choices.why: The helper will fix the problem, so the things will not stay there.
choices.misconception: Misses part of the direction

choices.text: Some things in the bins may be dirty or unsafe to touch.
choices.why: The helper uses gloves, which suggests the items may not be safe to touch with bare hands.

items.stem: What is the purpose of counting the bottles on Friday?

choices.text: To find out how many bins the team needs
choices.why: The team already knows it needs 3 bins.
choices.misconception: Confuses the purpose of a step

choices.text: To see which student brought the most bottles
choices.why: The talk does not compare students.
choices.misconception: Adds a purpose that was not said

choices.text: To find out if the new station helps the school recycle more
choices.why: The teacher says they want to see if the station makes a difference.

choices.text: To decide where to put the bins
choices.why: The bins are placed before Friday.
choices.misconception: Confuses the order and purpose of steps
